newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb generals, politicians trade insults.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb generals, politicians trade insults.

text.p: A power struggle between Bosnian Serb generals and political leaders intensified on Sunday after weekend talks failed to resolve a dispute over who would run the army.
Two days of discussions between Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic and top generals ended on Saturday without concrete agreement.
The standoff stems from Plavsic's decision to sack commander General Ratko Mladic and other top generals a week ago -- a move the army has so far refused to recognise.
The obscure officer named to replace Mladic, General Pero Colic, said civilian authorities were firmly in control and slammed the current general staff.

"This crisis is a crisis of individuals, sickly ambitious people who -- in the natural and imminent modernisation of the army -- do not see what they should as professionals and patriots," Bosnian Serb television quoted Colic as saying.
Bosnian Serb media, under the control of civilian authorities, also reported that army officers took control of a TV transmitter on Mount Zep in eastern Bosnia last Tuesday.
The seizure prevented Serb television, based in the governmment seat of Pale, from broadcasting to other towns in Bosnia's Serb republic.
Bosnian Serb television said a "group of dismissed generals and junior officers loyal to them seized the central television transmitter on Zep and disabled it".
Bosnian Serb civilian authorities ruled out resorting to violence but said they "must contemplate whether to take some of these so-called officers to court".
There was no response to the report from Bosnian Serb army headquarters in the northeastern village of Han Pijesak.
The mood was tense in Han Pijesak, which served as the army's base during 3-1/2 years of war in Bosnia.
Serb generals loyal to Mladic, an indicted war criminal who must step down under the Dayton peace agreement, insist the general staff should have a say over who will succeed him.
They scoff at newly-appointed commanders as unqualified party hacks.
Officers in the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia were following the standoff closely but declined to comment.
Diplomats say the West would be glad to see Mladic go but but fears the peace process could be damaged if the power struggle drags on.
As Bosnian Serb media heaped scorn on the army officers, a top general lashed out at the civilian authorities in a Belgrade newspaper interview.

"The conflict between the Interior Ministry and the army of the Serb republic is on the brink of an open conflict and threatens to become a genuine civil war," General Manojlo Milovanovic told Dnevni Telegraf.

Accusing political leaders of kow-towing to outside powers intent on "destroying" the Serb army and reunifying Bosnia as a single state, he said the army would obey civilian authorities only if it was sure Serb territory was "secure".
Bosnian Serb wartime leader Radovan Karadzic tried and failed to sack Mladic and other top generals last year.
In neighbouring Serbia, the patron of the Bosnian Serbs has kept silent but diplomats say the dismissals suit President Slobodan Milosevic.
The Serbian leader can take credit for cooperating with the Dayton agreement while Bosnian Serb civilian leaders will have to bear criticism from nationalists who revere Mladic.
